claims.text: HEA multilayers without explicit interlayers have suboptimal interface coherency.
Suboptimal interface coherency favors diffusion-mediated creep at elevated temperatures.
A few-nanometer TiC layer can be integrated between adjacent HEA layers by sputtering or laser deposition.
An ultrathin, epitaxially grown TiC interlayer will promote highly coherent TiC/HEA interfaces.
The proposed TiC/HEA interface will have low lattice mismatch.
A coherent TiC/HEA interface will suppress atomic diffusion across layer boundaries.
TiC's high melting point and robust bonding will reduce diffusivity along the interface.
Suppressing interfacial diffusion will shift creep from Nabarro–Herring or Coble creep toward dislocation-mediated creep.
After adding the TiC interlayer, stress will increasingly be accommodated by dislocation glide and climb rather than atomic diffusion.
Both diffusion and dislocation processes are active in the proposed HEA multilayers at approximately 500–700 °C under the selected constant stresses.
TiC-interlayered HEA multilayers will have lower creep strain rates than multilayers without TiC interlayers.
TiC-interlayered HEA multilayers will have higher yield strength than multilayers without TiC interlayers.
TiC-interlayered HEA multilayers will develop increased dislocation density at their interfaces.
Lower creep rates, higher yield strength, and increased interfacial dislocation density would indicate a transition from diffusion-controlled to dislocation-controlled creep.
HEA multilayers without TiC interlayers will show relatively higher creep rates because their interfaces are less coherent.
The beneficial creep-mechanism transition requires the TiC layer to maintain good coherency at a thickness of a few nanometers.
An excessively thick or poorly integrated TiC layer can generate misfit dislocations or partial coherence.
Misfit dislocations or partial coherence will diminish the proposed creep-mechanism transition.
